section_headings: Right heart catheterization and vasoreactivity testing  Recommendation Table 1

content.narrative_summary: This page presents selected revised (R) and new (N) recommendations comparing the 2015 and 2022 guideline versions in three tables: Right heart catheterization and vasoreactivity testing; Diagnostic strategy; and Screening and detection of pulmonary arterial hypertension and CTEPH.

recommendation_tables.title: Right heart catheterization and vasoreactivity testing  Recommendation Table 1

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that RHC comprises a complete set of haemodynamics and is performed following standardized protocols
Inhaled nitric oxide, inhaled iloprost, or i.v. epoprostenol are recommended for performing vasoreactivity testing

recommendation_tables.title: Diagnostic strategy  Recommendation Table 2

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to assign an echocardiographic probability of PH, based on an abnormal TRV and the presence of other echocardiographic signs suggestive of PH (see Table 10)
It is recommended to maintain the current threshold for TRV (>2.8 m/s) for echocardiographic probability of PH according to the updated haemodynamic definition
Based on the probability of PH by echocardiography, further testing should be considered in the clinical context (i.e. symptoms and risk factors or associated conditions for PAH/CTEPH)
In symptomatic patients with intermediate echocardiographic probability of PH, CPET may be considered to further determine the likelihood of PH

recommendation_tables.title: Screening and improved detection of pulmonary arterial hypertension and chronic thrombo-embolic pulmonary hypertension  Recommendation Table 3

rows.recommendation: In patients with SSc, an annual evaluation of the risk of having PAH is recommended
In adult patients with SSc of >3 years’ disease duration, an FVC ≥40%, and a DLCO <60%, the DETECT algorithm is recommended to identify asymptomatic patients with PAH
In patients with SSc, where breathlessness remains unexplained following non-invasive assessment, RHC is recommended to exclude PAH
Assessing the risk of having PAH, based on an evaluation of breathlessness, in combination with echocardiogram or PFTs and BNP/NT-proBNP, should be considered in patients with SSc
Policies to evaluate the risk of having PAH should be considered in hospitals managing patients with SSc
In symptomatic patients with SSc, exercise echocardiography or CPET, or CMR may be considered to aid decisions to perform RHC
In patients with CTD with overlap features of SSc, an annual evaluation of the risk of PAH may be considered
In patients with persistent or new-onset dyspnoea or exercise limitation following PE, further diagnostic evaluation to assess for CTEPH/CTEPD is recommended

rows.recommendation: For symptomatic patients with mismatched perfusion lung defects beyond 3�months of anticoagulation for acute PE, referral to a PH/CTEPH centre is recommended after considering the results of echocardiography, BNP/NT-proBNP, and/or CPET
Counselling regarding the risk of PAH, and annual screening is recommended for individuals who test positive for PAH-causing mutations and in first-degree relatives of patients with HPAH
In patients referred for liver transplantation, echocardiography is recommended as a screening test for PH
Further tests (echocardiography, BNP/NT-proBNP, PFTs, and/or CPET) should be considered in symptomatic patients with CTD, portal hypertension, or HIV to screen for PAH

recommendation_tables.title: Evaluating the disease severity and risk of death in patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension �096 Recommendation Table 4

rows.recommendation: For risk stratification at the time of diagnosis, the use of a three-strata model (low, intermediate, and high risk) is recommended, taking into account all available data including haemodynamics

For risk stratification during follow-up, the use of a four-strata model (low, intermediate–low, intermediate–high, and high risk) based on WHO–FC, 6MWD, and BNP/NT-proBNP is recommended, with additional variables taken into account as necessary
Achievement/maintenance of an intermediate-risk profile should be considered an inadequate treatment response for most patients with PAH
rows.supporting_text: In some PAH aetiologies and in patients with comorbidities, optimization of therapy should be considered on an individual basis while acknowledging that a low-risk profile is not always achievable

recommendation_tables.title: General measures and special circumstances �096 Recommendation Table 5

rows.recommendation: Supervised exercise training should be considered in physically deconditioned PAH patients under medical therapy
rows.supporting_text: Supervised exercise training is recommended in patients with PAH under medical therapy

rows.recommendation: Immunization of PAH patients against influenza and pneumococcal infection is recommended
rows.supporting_text: Immunization of patients with PAH against SARS-CoV-2, influenza, and Streptococcus pneumoniae is recommended

rows.recommendation: Correction of anaemia and/or iron status may be considered in PAH patients
rows.supporting_text: In the presence of iron-deficiency anaemia, correction of iron status is recommended in patients with PAH

rows.recommendation: In the absence of anaemia, iron repletion may be considered in patients with PAH with iron deficiency
Oral anticoagulant treatment may be considered in patients with IPAH, HPAH, and PAH due to use of anorexigens
rows.supporting_text: Anticoagulation is not generally recommended in patients with PAH but may be considered on an individual basis

rows.recommendation: The use of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin-2 receptor antagonists, beta-blockers, and ivabradine is not recommended in patients with PAH unless required by comorbidities (i.e. high blood pressure, coronary artery disease, or left HF)
rows.supporting_text: The use of ACEis, ARBs, ARNis, SGLT-2is, beta-blockers, or ivabradine is not recommended in patients with PAH unless required by comorbidities (i.e. high blood pressure, coronary artery disease, left HF, or arrhythmias)

rows.recommendation: In-flight O2 administration should be considered for patients in WHO-FC III and IV and those with arterial blood O2 pressure consistently <8 kPa (60 mmHg)
rows.supporting_text: In-flight O2 administration is recommended for patients using oxygen or whose arterial blood oxygen pressure is <8 kPa (60 mmHg) at sea level

rows.recommendation: In elective surgery, epidural rather than general anaesthesia should be preferred whenever possible
rows.supporting_text: For interventions requiring anaesthesia, multidisciplinary consultation at a PH centre to assess risk and benefit should be considered

section_headings: Women of childbearing potential – Recommendation Table 6

content.narrative_summary: This page presents three recommendation tables addressing management of (1) women of childbearing potential with PAH, (2) vasoreactive PAH patients, and (3) non-vasoreactive PAH patients without cardiopulmonary comorbidities.

recommendation_tables.title: Women of childbearing potential – Recommendation Table 6

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that women of childbearing potential with PAH are counselled at the time of diagnosis about the risks and uncertainties associated with becoming pregnant; this should include advice against becoming pregnant, and referral for psychological support where needed

It is recommended that women of childbearing potential with PAH be provided with clear contraceptive advice, considering the individual needs of the woman but recognizing that the implications of contraceptive failure are significant in PAH

It is recommended that women with PAH who consider pregnancy or who become pregnant receive prompt counselling in an experienced PH centre to facilitate genetic counselling and shared decision-making, and to provide psychological support to the patients and their families where needed
For women with PAH having termination of pregnancy, it is recommended that this be performed in PH centres, with psychological support provided to the patient and her family
For women with PAH who desire to have children, where available, adoption and surrogacy with pre-conception genetic counselling may be considered
As teratogenic potential has been reported in preclinical models for endothelin receptor antagonists and riociguat, these drugs are not recommended during pregnancy

recommendation_tables.title: Treatment of vasoreactive patients with idiopathic, heritable, or drug-associated pulmonary arterial hypertension – Recommendation Table 7

rows.recommendation: Continuing high doses of CCBs is recommended in patients with IPAH, HPAH, or DPAH in WHO-FC I or II with marked haemodynamic improvement (mPAP <30 mmHg and PVR <4 WU)
In patients with a positive vasoreactivity test but insufficient long-term response to CCBs who require additional PAH therapy, continuation of CCB therapy should be considered

recommendation_tables.title: Treatment of non-vasoreactive patients with idiopathic, heritable, or drug-associated pulmonary arterial hypertension who present without cardiopulmonary comorbidities – Recommendation Table 8

rows.recommendation: In patients with IPAH/HPAH/DPAH who present at high risk of death, initial combination therapy with a PDE5i, an ERA, and i.v./s.c. prostacyclin analogues should be considered
In patients with IPAH/HPAH/DPAH who present at intermediate–low risk of death while receiving ERA/PDE5i therapy, the addition of selexipag should be considered

In patients with IPAH/HPAH/DPAH who present at intermediate–high or high risk of death while receiving ERA/PDE5i therapy, the addition of i.v./s.c. prostacyclin analogues and referral for lung transplantation (LTx) evaluation should be considered

recommendation_tables.title: Continuation of previous recommendation table

rows.recommendation: In patients with IPAH/HPAH/DPAH who present at intermediate–low risk of death while receiving ERA/PDE5i therapy, switching from PDE5i to riociguat may be considered

recommendation_tables.title: Initial oral drug combination therapy for patients with idiopathic, heritable, or drug-associated pulmonary arterial hypertension without cardiopulmonary comorbidities – Recommendation Table 9

rows.recommendation: Initial combination therapy with ambrisentan and tadalafil is recommended
Initial combination therapy with macitentan and tadalafil is recommended
Initial combination therapy with other ERAs and PDE5is should be considered
Initial combination therapy with macitentan, tadalafil, and selexipag is not recommended

recommendation_tables.title: Sequential drug combination therapy for patients with idiopathic, heritable, or drug-associated pulmonary arterial hypertension – Recommendation Table 10

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to base treatment escalations on risk assessment and general treatment strategies (see treatment algorithm)
The addition of macitentan to PDE5is or oral/inhaled prostacyclin analogues is recommended to reduce the risk of morbidity/mortality events
The addition of oral treprostinil to ERA or PDE5i/riociguat monotherapy is recommended to reduce the risk of morbidity/mortality events
The addition of bosentan to sildenafil is not recommended to reduce the risk of morbidity/mortality events
The addition of riociguat to bosentan should be considered to improve exercise capacity

recommendation_tables.title: Treatment of non-vasoreactive patients with idiopathic, heritable, or drug-associated pulmonary arterial hypertension who present with cardiopulmonary comorbidities – Recommendation Table 11

rows.recommendation: In patients with IPAH/HPAH/DPAH and cardiopulmonary comorbidities, initial monotherapy with a PDE5i or an ERA should be considered

In patients with IPAH/HPAH/DPAH with cardiopulmonary comorbidities who present at intermediate or high risk of death while receiving PDE5i or ERA monotherapy, additional PAH medication may be considered on an individual basis

recommendation_tables.title: Efficacy of intensive care management for pulmonary arterial hypertension – Recommendation Table 12

rows.recommendation: When managing patients with right HF in the ICU, it is recommended to involve physicians with expertise, treat causative factors, and use supportive measures including inotropes and vasopressors, fluid management, and PAH drugs as appropriate

Mechanical circulatory support may be an option for selected patients as a bridge to transplantation or to recovery, and interhospital transfer should be considered if such resources are unavailable on site

content.narrative_summary: This page presents Recommendation Tables 13–17 covering lung transplantation and pulmonary arterial hypertension associated with drugs or toxins, connective tissue disease, HIV infection, and portal hypertension.

recommendation_tables.title: Lung transplantation – Recommendation Table 13

rows.recommendation: Lung transplantation is recommended soon after inadequate clinical response on maximal medical therapy
rows.supporting_text: It is recommended that potentially eligible candidates are referred for LTx evaluation when they have an inadequate response to oral combination therapy, indicated by an intermediate–high or high risk or by a REVEAL risk score >7

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to list patients for LTx who present with a high risk of death or with a REVEAL risk score ≥10 despite receiving optimized medical therapy, including s.c. or i.v. prostacyclin analogues

recommendation_tables.title: Pulmonary arterial hypertension associated with drugs or toxins – Recommendation Table 14

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to make a diagnosis of drug- or toxin-associated PAH in patients who had relevant exposure and in whom other causes of PH have been excluded
In patients with suspected drug- or toxin-associated PAH, it is recommended to discontinue the causative agent immediately whenever possible
Immediate PAH therapy should be considered in patients who present with intermediate/high-risk PAH at diagnosis
Patients with low-risk PAH should be re-evaluated 3–4 months after discontinuing the suspected drug or toxin, and PAH therapy may be considered when the haemodynamics have not normalized

recommendation_tables.title: Pulmonary arterial hypertension associated with connective tissue disease – Recommendation Table 15

rows.recommendation: In patients with PAH associated with CTD, treatment of the underlying condition according to current guidelines is recommended

recommendation_tables.title: Pulmonary arterial hypertension associated with human immunodeficiency virus infection – Recommendation Table 16

rows.recommendation: In patients with PAH associated with HIV infection, antiretroviral treatment according to current guidelines is recommended

In patients with PAH associated with HIV infection, initial monotherapy should be considered, followed by sequential combination if necessary, taking into consideration comorbidities and drug–drug interactions

recommendation_tables.title: Pulmonary arterial hypertension associated with portal hypertension – Recommendation Table 17

rows.recommendation: Echocardiographic assessment for signs of PH is recommended in symptomatic patients with liver disease or portal hypertension and in all candidates for liver transplantation
rows.supporting_text: Echocardiography is recommended in patients with liver disease or portal hypertension with signs or symptoms suggestive of PH, and as a screening tool in patients evaluated for liver transplantation or transjugular portosystemic shunt

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that the treatment algorithm for patients with other forms of PAH should be applied to patients with PAH associated with portal hypertension, taking into account the severity of liver disease
rows.supporting_text: In patients with PAH associated with portal hypertension, initial monotherapy should be considered, followed by sequential combination if necessary, taking into consideration the underlying liver disease and indication for liver transplantation

rows.recommendation: Liver transplantation may be considered in selected patients responding well to PAH therapy
rows.supporting_text: Liver transplantation should be considered on an individual basis in patients with PAH associated with portal hypertension, as long as PVR is normal or near normal with PAH therapy

content.narrative_summary: This page contains recommendation tables for various forms of pulmonary hypertension: Table 18 (shunt closure based on pulmonary–systemic flow ratio), Table 19 (PAH associated with adult congenital heart disease), Table 20 (PAH with signs of venous/capillary involvement), and the beginning of Table 21 (paediatric pulmonary hypertension).

recommendation_tables.title: Shunt closure in patients with pulmonary–systemic flow ratio >1.5:1 based on calculated pulmonary vascular resistance – Recommendation Table 18

rows.recommendation: In patients with ASD, VSD, or PDA and a PVR <3 WU, shunt closure is recommended
In patients with ASD, VSD, or PDA and a PVR of 3–5 WU, shunt closure should be considered
In patients with ASD and a PVR >5 WU that declines to <5 WU with PAH treatment, shunt closure may be considered
In patients with VSD or PDA and a PVR >5 WU, shunt closure may be considered after careful evaluation in specialized centres
In patients with ASD and a PVR >5 WU despite PAH treatment, shunt closure is not recommended

recommendation_tables.title: Pulmonary arterial hypertension associated with adult congenital heart disease – Recommendation Table 19

rows.recommendation: Risk assessment is recommended for patients with persistent PAH after defect closure
Risk assessment should be considered in patients with Eisenmenger syndrome
Bosentan is recommended in WHO-FC III patients with Eisenmenger syndrome
rows.supporting_text: Bosentan is recommended in symptomatic patients with Eisenmenger syndrome to improve exercise capacity

rows.recommendation: The use of supplemental iron treatment may be considered in patients with low ferritin plasma levels
rows.supporting_text: Supplemental iron treatment should be considered in patients with iron deficiency

rows.recommendation: Combination drug therapy may be considered in patients with Eisenmenger syndrome
rows.supporting_text: In patients with PAH after corrected adult CHD, initial oral combination therapy with drugs approved for PAH should be considered for patients at low and intermediate risk, while initial combination therapy including i.v./s.c. prostacyclin analogues should be considered for patients at high risk

rows.recommendation: Combination drug therapy may be considered in patients with Eisenmenger syndrome
rows.supporting_text: In patients with adult CHD, including Eisenmenger syndrome, sequential combination therapy should be considered if patients do not meet treatment goals

rows.recommendation: In women with Eisenmenger syndrome, pregnancy is not recommended
If symptoms of hyperviscosity are present, phlebotomy with isovolumic replacement should be considered, usually when the haematocrit is >65%
rows.supporting_text: In patients with Eisenmenger syndrome, routine phlebotomy to lower elevated haematocrit is not recommended

recommendation_tables.title: Pulmonary arterial hypertension with signs of venous/capillary involvement – Recommendation Table 20

rows.recommendation: A combination of clinical findings, physical examination, bronchoscopy, and radiological findings is recommended to diagnose PVOD/PCH
rows.supporting_text: A combination of clinical and radiological findings, ABG, PFTs, and genetic testing is recommended to diagnose PAH with signs of venous and/or capillary involvement (PVOD/PCH)

rows.recommendation: In patients with PVOD/PCH, the use of drugs approved for PAH may be considered with careful monitoring of clinical symptoms and gas exchange
Lung biopsy is not recommended to confirm a diagnosis of PVOD/PCH

recommendation_tables.title: Paediatric pulmonary hypertension – Recommendation Table 21

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to perform the diagnostic work-up, including RHC and acute vasoreactivity testing, and treat children with PH at centres with specific expertise in paediatric PH

section_headings: Pulmonary hypertension associated with left heart disease – Recommendation Table 22
content.narrative_summary: This page continues recommendation tables for paediatric pulmonary hypertension and begins Recommendation Table 22 on pulmonary hypertension associated with left heart disease. The tables are continued from the previous page and continue onto the next page.

rows.recommendation: A PH diagnostic algorithm work-up is recommended for diagnosis and definition of the specific aetiology group in paediatric PH patients
In children with PH, a comprehensive work-up for confirming diagnosis and specific aetiology is recommended (similar to that in adults, but adapted for age)
For confirming PH diagnosis, RHC is recommended, preferably before initiating any PAH therapy
In children with IPAH/HPAH, acute vasoreactivity testing is recommended to detect those who may benefit from calcium channel blocker therapy

It is recommended to define a positive response to acute vasoreactivity testing in children similar to adults by a reduction of mPAP ≥ 10 mmHg to reach an absolute value of mPAP ≤ 40 mmHg, with an increased or unchanged CO
A PAH-specific therapeutic algorithm is recommended in paediatric PH patients
In children with PAH, a therapeutic strategy based on risk stratification and treatment response is recommended, extrapolated from that in adults but adapted for age
Specific paediatric determinants of risk should be considered

It is recommended to monitor the treatment response in children with PAH by serially assessing a panel of data derived from clinical assessment, echocardiographic evaluation, biochemical markers, and exercise tolerance tests
Achieving and maintaining a low-risk profile should be considered as an adequate treatment response for children with PAH
It is recommended to screen infants with bronchopulmonary dysplasia for PH

In infants with (or at risk of) bronchopulmonary dysplasia and PH, treating lung disease, including hypoxia, aspiration, and structural airway disease, and optimizing respiratory support is recommended before initiating PAH therapy

In neonates and infants, a diagnostic and therapeutic approach to PH distinct from that in older children and adults should be considered, given the frequent association with developmental vascular and parenchymal lung disease

recommendation_tables.title: Pulmonary hypertension associated with left heart disease – Recommendation Table 22

rows.recommendation: RHC is recommended for suspected PH in patients with LHD, if it aids management decisions
RHC is recommended in patients with severe tricuspid regurgitation with or without LHD prior to surgical or interventional valve repair

Patients with PH-LHD and a severe pre-capillary component as indicated by a high DPG and/or high PVR should be referred to an expert PH centre for a complete diagnostic work-up and an individual treatment decision
In patients with LHD and CpcPH with a severe pre-capillary component (e.g. PVR > 5 WU), an individualized approach to treatment is recommended

When patients with PH and multiple risk factors for LHD, who have a normal PAWP at rest but an abnormal response to exercise or fluid challenge, are treated with PAH drugs, close monitoring is recommended

section_headings: Pulmonary hypertension associated with lung disease and/or hypoxia – Recommendation Table 23
Chronic thrombo-embolic pulmonary hypertension and chronic thrombo-embolic pulmonary disease without pulmonary hypertension – Recommendation Table 24
content.narrative_summary: This page presents two recommendation tables. Table 23 covers pulmonary hypertension associated with lung disease and/or hypoxia, including diagnostic assessment by echocardiography, referral, right heart catheterization, and use of targeted therapies. Table 24 addresses management of chronic thrombo-embolic pulmonary hypertension and chronic thrombo-embolic pulmonary disease without pulmonary hypertension, including anticoagulation, operability assessment, pulmonary endarterectomy, balloon pulmonary angioplasty, and riociguat.

recommendation_tables.title: Pulmonary hypertension associated with lung disease and/or hypoxia – Recommendation Table 23

rows.supporting_text: In patients with PH at RHC, a borderline PAWP (13–15 mmHg) and features of HFpEF, additional testing with exercise or fluid challenge may be considered to uncover post-capillary PH

rows.recommendation: Echocardiography is recommended for the non-invasive diagnostic assessment of suspected PH in patients with lung disease
rows.supporting_text: If PH is suspected in patients with lung disease, it is recommended that echocardiography be performed and the results interpreted in conjunction with ABG, PFTs including DLCO, and CT imaging

rows.recommendation: Optimal treatment of the underlying lung disease, including long-term O₂ therapy in patients with chronic hypoxaemia, is recommended in patients with PH due to lung diseases
rows.supporting_text: In patients with lung disease and suspected PH, it is recommended to optimize treatment of the underlying lung disease and, where indicated, hypoxaemia, sleep-disordered breathing, and/or alveolar hypoventilation

rows.recommendation: Referral to an expert centre is recommended in patients with echocardiographic signs of severe PH and/or severe right ventricular dysfunction
rows.supporting_text: In patients with lung disease and suspected severe PH, or where there is uncertainty regarding the treatment of PH, referral to a PH centre is recommended
In patients with lung disease and severe PH, an individualized approach to treatment is recommended
It is recommended to refer eligible patients with lung disease and PH for LTx evaluation

rows.recommendation: RHC is not recommended for suspected PH in patients with lung disease, unless therapeutic consequences are to be expected (e.g. LTx, alternative diagnoses such as PAH or CTEPH, and potential enrolment in a clinical trial)
rows.supporting_text: In patients with lung disease and suspected PH, RHC is recommended if the results are expected to aid management decisions
Inhaled treprostinil may be considered in patients with PH associated with ILD
The use of ambrisentan is not recommended in patients with PH associated with IPF
The use of riociguat is not recommended in patients with PH associated with IIP

recommendation_tables.title: Chronic thrombo-embolic pulmonary hypertension and chronic thrombo-embolic pulmonary disease without pulmonary hypertension – Recommendation Table 24

rows.recommendation: Lifelong anticoagulation is recommended in all patients with CTEPH
rows.supporting_text: Lifelong therapeutic doses of anticoagulation are recommended in all patients with CTEPH

rows.recommendation: Antiphospholipid syndrome testing is recommended in patients with CTEPH
In patients with CTEPH and antiphospholipid syndrome, anticoagulation with VKAs is recommended
It is recommended that all patients with CTEPH receive assessment of operability and decisions regarding other treatment strategies made by a multidisciplinary team of experts
rows.supporting_text: It is recommended that all patients with CTEPH are reviewed by a CTEPH team for the assessment of multimodality management

rows.recommendation: Surgical PEA in deep hypothermia circulatory arrest is recommended for patients with CTEPH

content.narrative_summary: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) affects all age groups globally, with an estimated prevalence of ~1% of the population and higher prevalence in individuals over 65 years of age. Left heart disease is the leading cause of PH worldwide, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is the second most common cause. In the UK, PH prevalence has doubled over the past decade to 125 cases per million inhabitants. Regardless of etiology, PH is associated with worsening symptoms and increased mortality. In developing countries, congenital heart disease, schistosomiasis, HIV infection, and high altitude are important but understudied causes. Registry data from developed countries indicate an incidence of ~6 and a prevalence of 48–55 cases per million adults for PAH, predominantly affecting younger females, though recently more older patients (≥65 years) are diagnosed with a more equal sex distribution. Idiopathic PAH is the most common subtype (50–60%), followed by PAH associated with connective tissue disease, congenital heart disease, and porto-pulmonary hypertension. Exposure to drugs and toxins is associated with PAH; the association is classified as definite or possible based on the Sixth WSPH criteria, with definite associations supported by outbreaks and case-control or large series studies, and possible associations suggested by case series.

section_headings: 5.1.4. Pulmonary function tests and arterial blood gases
content.narrative_summary: Chest radiography in pulmonary hypertension typically shows right atrial/right ventricular enlargement and pulmonary artery enlargement, although a normal chest X-ray does not exclude the diagnosis; signs of left heart disease or lung disease may also be present. Pulmonary function tests (forced spirometry, body plethysmography, DLCO) and arterial blood gas analysis are required to distinguish PH groups, assess comorbidities and determine disease severity. PFTs are often normal or show mild restrictive/obstructive changes; more severe abnormalities occur in PH associated with congenital heart disease or interstitial lung disease. DLCO is usually mildly reduced, markedly so (<45% predicted) in certain forms and portends poorer prognosis. Arterial PaO2 is typically normal or slightly reduced, with severe reduction suggesting shunt lesions; PaCO2 is generally low due to hyperventilation.

section_headings: 5.1.7. Non-contrast and contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography examinations, and digital subtraction angiography
content.narrative_summary: The page discusses the presence of chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) in 7–10% of patients with pulmonary veno‐occlusive disease/pulmonary capillary hemangiomatosis (PVOD/PCH) or pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), and notes that deposition of perfusion agent in extrapulmonary organs may indicate right-to-left shunting. It then describes computed tomography (CT) imaging signs suggestive of pulmonary hypertension, including enlarged pulmonary artery diameter, PA-to-aorta ratio >0.9, PA diameter ≥30 mm, RVOT wall thickness ≥6 mm, and septal deviation ≥140° (or RV:LV ratio ≥1), and highlights CT’s role in identifying features of parenchymal lung disease and PVOD/PCH. The section reviews the use of computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) to detect CTEPH—such as intraluminal defects, webs, bands, mosaic perfusion, and enlarged bronchial arteries—its diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity 76%, specificity 96%), and its use for detecting other cardiovascular abnormalities including intracardiac shunts, abnormal pulmonary venous return, patent ductus arteriosus, and pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (PAVMs).

content.narrative_summary: Patients with advanced or decompensated PH (WHO-FC III/IV) presenting with right ventricular failure, syncope, low cardiac output, arrhythmias, or hemodynamic instability require immediate inpatient evaluation and referral to a specialized pulmonary hypertension center. content.narrative_summary: The 6-minute walking test (6MWT) is the most widely used measure of exercise capacity in pulmonary hypertension. It is easy to perform, inexpensive, and validated but influenced by factors such as sex, age, height, weight, comorbidities, oxygen needs, learning curve, and motivation. Results are reported as absolute distance and are used as primary or secondary endpoints in clinical trials. Threshold values of 165 m and 440 m predict 1-year mortality and survival, respectively. Improvements in 6MWD are less predictive than clinical outcomes. The incremental shuttle walking test (ISWT) offers a maximal alternative without a ceiling effect, and cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) remains a comprehensive but less accessible test in PAH.

section_headings: 6.2.7. Comprehensive prognostic evaluation, risk assessment, and treatment goals
content.narrative_summary: This section discusses the evolution of risk stratification in pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) from a three-strata model to a simplified four-strata model (low, intermediate–low, intermediate–high, high risk), highlighting the prognostic value of WHO functional class (WHO-FC), 6-minute walk distance (6MWD), and BNP/NT-proBNP levels. Registry data showed higher-than-predicted mortality in intermediate and high risk groups, leading to updated cut-offs and validation of the four-strata model across multiple PAH registries. Limitations of earlier tools and the importance of incorporating additional biomarkers and haemodynamics are noted, along with guidance on using at least three variables (WHO-FC, 6MWD, BNP/NT-proBNP) for risk stratification.

content.narrative_summary: Pregnancy in women with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) carries high maternal and neonatal mortality despite improved management, and pre-pregnancy counseling, multidisciplinary care, and therapy adjustments (e.g., stopping endothelin receptor antagonists) are recommended. Contraception should be individualized, with clear advice on highly effective methods and consideration of implants, intrauterine devices, or sterilization, noting peri-operative risks. Surgical procedures in PAH have increased peri-operative mortality influenced by PH severity; decisions should involve a multidisciplinary PH team with individualized risk–benefit assessments and optimized PAH therapy. Travel and altitude exposure may induce hypoxaemia and pulmonary vasoconstriction; short-term hypoxia is generally tolerated but supplemental oxygen and travel planning—including medications, extra doses, and PH center contacts—are advised for altitudes >1500 m or when PaO₂ <8 kPa.

content.narrative_summary: Patients with PAH who respond favorably to acute vasoreactivity testing may have a long-term response to calcium channel blockers (CCBs), though less than 10% of patients with IPAH, HPAH, or DPAH are responders and an acute response does not guarantee long-term benefit in other forms of PAH. Nifedipine, diltiazem, and amlodipine are the CCBs most commonly used; amlodipine and felodipine are increasingly used due to tolerability but require high, progressively titrated doses. The main adverse effects are systemic hypotension and peripheral oedema. Patients meeting acute response criteria and treated with CCBs require close follow-up with reassessment after 3–6 months, including right heart catheterization, and additional vasoreactivity testing if needed. Those with WHO-FC I/II and marked hemodynamic improvement (mPAP <30 mmHg and PVR <4 WU) on CCBs may continue; those without satisfactory response should start PAH therapy, and in some cases combination therapy may be required.

content.title: 7.4. Pulmonary arterial hypertension associated with portal hypertension
section_headings: 7.4. Pulmonary arterial hypertension associated with portal hypertension
content.narrative_summary: Pulmonary arterial hypertension develops in 2–6% of patients with portal hypertension (PoPH) and represents 5–15% of PAH cases. PoPH is distinct from hepatopulmonary syndrome and may occur with or without liver disease. Diagnosis is based on unexplained pre-capillary PH in patients with portal hypertension or portosystemic shunts; transthoracic echocardiography is the first screening step, with right heart catheterization required to confirm PAH (elevated PVR). Therapy follows general PAH principles, considering liver disease severity and potential drug effects. Although PoPH patients are often excluded from trials, registry data support the use of approved PAH therapies (mostly PDE5 inhibitors and ERAs) with improvements in haemodynamics, functional class, 6MWD, and biomarkers; a randomized trial of macitentan (PORTICO) showed significant PVR reduction. Liver transplantation is not an indication per se but may be feasible if hemodynamic targets (mPAP <35 mmHg and PVR <5 WU, or mPAP ≥35 mmHg and PVR <3 WU) are met; mPAP ≥45 mmHg remains a contraindication.

section_headings: 7.5. Pulmonary arterial hypertension associated with adult congenital heart disease
content.narrative_summary: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) in adults with congenital heart disease (CHD) negatively impacts prognosis and clinical status. It is categorized as Group 1 PH and requires exclusion of post-capillary causes. CHD-associated PAH is heterogeneous, with segmental PH in complex lesions. Approximately 3–7% of adults with CHD develop PAH, more often in females, and prevalence after simple defect correction is ~3%. Eisenmenger syndrome presents with chronic hypoxaemia, cyanosis, secondary erythrocytosis, thrombocytopenia and multi-organ involvement. Diagnosis relies on symptoms, history, physical exam, PFTs, ABG, echocardiography, exercise/laboratory tests and right heart catheterization with Qp/Qs measurement. Thermodilution may overestimate pulmonary vascular resistance in shunts. Predictors of poor outcome include WHO-FC III–IV, reduced 6MWD or peak VO₂, prior hospitalization, elevated biomarkers (NT-proBNP >500 pg/mL, CRP >10 mg/L), organ dysfunction and echocardiographic RV indices. Eisenmenger patients have relatively stable long-term course but still carry risks; specific risk factors include degree of shunting, age, oxygen saturation and pericardial effusion.

content.narrative_summary: This section reviews management of adult congenital heart disease (CHD)–associated pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), emphasizing specialized multidisciplinary care, patient education, and psychosocial support. Surgical or interventional shunt closure is considered only in selected patients with systemic-to-pulmonary shunts and appropriate hemodynamics, but is contraindicated in Eisenmenger syndrome. Theoretical risks of paradoxical embolism with prostacyclin analogues are noted. The limited evidence for treatment in patients with small shunts or segmental PH is outlined. Pregnancy requires specialized care and contraception is advised. Iron supplementation and phlebotomy guidelines are described, and heart–lung transplantation is presented as a last‐resort option.

section_headings: 9. Pulmonary hypertension associated with lung diseases and/or hypoxia (group 3)
content.narrative_summary: Section 9 begins by noting that pulmonary hypertension (PH) frequently occurs in patients with COPD, emphysema, ILD, combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema (CPFE), and hypoventilation syndromes. PH is uncommon in obstructive sleep apnoea unless other conditions coexist. Hypoxia-induced PH at high altitude may affect >5% of the population, with genetic factors contributing. section_headings: 11. Pulmonary hypertension with unclear and/or multifactorial mechanisms (group 5)
content.narrative_summary: Pulmonary hypertension group 5 comprises conditions with unclear and/or multifactorial mechanisms that may involve complex and overlapping pulmonary vascular involvement. Although less-studied, it represents a significant worldwide burden and includes haematological disorders (e.g., sickle cell disease, β-thalassaemia, chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms), systemic disorders (e.g., sarcoidosis), metabolic diseases (e.g., glycogen storage disease), and others (e.g., chronic renal failure, pulmonary tumour thrombotic microangiopathy, fibrosing mediastinitis). Contributing factors may include hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, pulmonary vascular remodelling, thrombosis, fibrotic destruction or extrinsic vascular compression, pulmonary vasculitis, high-output cardiac failure, and left heart failure. Patients require careful assessment and treatment directed to the underlying condition. Section 11.1 begins a detailed discussion of haematological disorders.

content.narrative_summary: The section defines the concept and importance of a specialized pulmonary hypertension (PH) centre, highlighting that severe forms of PH (such as PAH and CTEPH) require highly specialized, multidisciplinary management. In patients with suspected drug- or toxin-associated PAH, it is recommended to immediately discontinue the causative agent whenever possible
In patients with PAH associated with CTD, treatment of the underlying condition according to current guidelines is recommended
In patients with PAH associated with CTD, the same treatment algorithm as for patients with IPAH is recommended
In patients with PAH associated with HIV infection, antiretroviral treatment according to current guidelines is recommended

Echocardiography is recommended in patients with liver disease or portal hypertension with signs or symptoms suggestive of PH, and as a screening tool in patients evaluated for liver transplantation or transjugular portosystemic shunt
It is recommended that patients with PAH associated with portal hypertension are referred to centres with expertise in managing both conditions
Drugs approved for PAH are not recommended for patients with portal hypertension and unclassified PH (i.e. elevated mPAP, high CO, and a normal PVR)

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for pulmonary arterial hypertension associated with adult congenital heart disease – Treatment

rows.recommendation: Bosentan is recommended in symptomatic patients with Eisenmenger syndrome to improve exercise capacity
In women with Eisenmenger syndrome, pregnancy is not recommended

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for pulmonary arterial hypertension with signs of venous/capillary involvement

rows.recommendation: A combination of clinical and radiological findings, ABG, PFTs, and genetic testing is recommended to diagnose PAH with signs of venous and/or capillary involvement (PVOD/PCH)
Identification of biallelic EIF2AK4 mutations is recommended to confirm a diagnosis of heritable PVOD/PCH
Referral of eligible patients with PVOD/PCH to a transplant centre for evaluation is recommended as soon as the diagnosis is established
Lung biopsy is not recommended to confirm a diagnosis of PVOD/PCH

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for paediatric pulmonary hypertension – Children

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to perform the diagnostic work-up, including RHC and acute vasoreactivity testing, and treat children with PH at centres with specific expertise in paediatric PH
In children with PH, a comprehensive work-up for confirming diagnosis and specific aetiology is recommended (similar to that in adults, but adapted for age)
For confirming PH diagnosis, RHC is recommended, preferably before initiating any PAH therapy
In children with IPAH/PAH, acute vasoreactivity testing is recommended to detect those who may benefit from CCB therapy

It is recommended to similarly define a positive response to acute vasoreactivity testing in children and adults by a reduction in mPAP ≥10 mmHg to reach an absolute value of mPAP ≤40 mmHg, with an increased or unchanged CO
In children with PAH, a therapeutic strategy based on risk stratification and treatment response is recommended, extrapolated from that in adults, but adapted for age

It is recommended to monitor the treatment response in children with PAH by serially assessing a panel of data derived from clinical assessment, echocardiographic evaluation, biochemical markers, and exercise tolerance tests

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for paediatric pulmonary hypertension – Infants

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to screen infants with bronchopulmonary dysplasia for PH

In infants with (or at risk of) bronchopulmonary dysplasia and PH, treating lung disease—including hypoxia, aspiration, and structural airway disease—and optimizing respiratory support is recommended before initiating PAH therapy

rows.recommendation: In patients with LHD, optimizing treatment of the underlying condition is recommended before considering assessment of suspected PH
RHC is recommended for suspected PH in patients with LHD, if it aids management decisions

content.narrative_summary: This page presents multiple recommendation tables outlining recommendations and non-recommendations for pulmonary hypertension in various contexts: left heart disease, lung disease and/or hypoxia, chronic thrombo-embolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH), and for pulmonary hypertension centres. Each recommendation is accompanied by its Class of Recommendation (COR) and Level of Evidence (LOE).

rows.recommendation: RHC is recommended in patients with severe tricuspid regurgitation with or without LHD prior to surgical or interventional valve repair
For patients with LHD and suspected PH with features of a severe pre-capillary component and/or markers of RV dysfunction, referral to a PH centre for a complete diagnostic work-up is recommended
In patients with LHD and CpcPH with a severe pre-capillary component (e.g. PVR >5 WU), an individualized approach to treatment is recommended

When patients with PH and multiple risk factors for LHD, who have a normal PAWP at rest but an abnormal response to exercise or fluid challenge, are treated with PAH drugs, close monitoring is recommended
Drugs approved for PAH are not recommended in PH-LHD

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for pulmonary hypertension associated with lung disease and/or hypoxia

rows.recommendation: If PH is suspected in patients with lung disease, it is recommended that echocardiography be performed and results interpreted in conjunction with ABG, PFTs including DLCO, and CT imaging

In patients with lung disease and suspected PH, it is recommended to optimize treatment of the underlying lung disease and, where indicated, hypoxaemia, sleep-disordered breathing, and/or alveolar hypoventilation
In patients with lung disease and suspected severe PH, or where there is uncertainty regarding the treatment of PH, referral to a PH centre is recommended
In patients with lung disease and severe PH, an individualized approach to treatment is recommended
It is recommended to refer eligible patients with lung disease and PH for LTx evaluation
In patients with lung disease and suspected PH, RHC is recommended if the results are expected to aid management decisions
The use of ambrisentan is not recommended in patients with PH associated with IPF
The use of riociguat is not recommended in patients with PH associated with IIP
The use of PAH medication is not recommended in patients with lung disease and non-severe PH

recommendation_tables.title: CTEPH

rows.recommendation: Lifelong, therapeutic doses of anticoagulation are recommended in all patients with CTEPH
Antiphospholipid syndrome testing is recommended in patients with CTEPH
In patients with CTEPH and antiphospholipid syndrome, anticoagulation with VKAs is recommended
It is recommended that all patients with CTEPH are reviewed by a CTEPH team for the assessment of multimodality management
PEA is recommended as the treatment of choice for patients with CTEPH and fibrotic obstructions within pulmonary arteries accessible by surgery
BPA is recommended in patients who are technically inoperable or have residual PH after PEA and distal obstructions amenable to BPA
Riociguat is recommended for symptomatic patients with inoperable CTEPH or persistent/recurrent PH after PEA
Long-term follow-up is recommended after PEA and BPA, as well as for patients with CTEPH established on medical therapy

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for pulmonary hypertension centres

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that PH centres provide care by a multidisciplinary team (cardiologist, pneumonologist, rheumatologist, nurse specialist, radiologist, psychological and social work support, appropriate on-call expertise)
It is recommended that PH centres have direct links and quick referral patterns to other services (such as genetic counselling, PEA/BPA, LTx, adult congenital heart disease service)
